analogy.p: A football team has players who all have the same basic skills, but at the start of a season each takes a specialised role: goalkeeper, defender, striker. The goalkeeper has gloves and stands in goal (a special structure for a special job), and the team is far more effective than if everyone tried to do everything. In the same way cells differentiate to carry out different functions, and the organism works better because of it. The analogy breaks down because players can change positions during a match, while most differentiated animal cells cannot change type.

bullets: **Differentiation** is the process by which a cell changes to become specialised for its job.
As an organism develops, cells differentiate to form different types of cell, each with a particular **function**.
In most **animals**, cells differentiate at an early stage of development; in mature animals, cell division is mainly for **repair and replacement**.
In **plants**, many types of cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.
Know named examples: **sperm, nerve, muscle, root hair, xylem and phloem** cells, and be ready for ciliated epithelial, palisade, red blood and others.
Link to other topics: levels of organisation, stem cells, meristems, mitosis, transport in plants and respiration.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8461 (4.1.2.1 Cell differentiation, with specialised cells met in 4.1.1 and 4.2.2) expects you to explain what **differentiation** is, to know that cells **specialise** to carry out particular functions, and to explain how the **structure of different types of cell is related to their function** in a given context. It also expects you to know the difference between animals and plants in how long cells can keep differentiating. Questions give you an unfamiliar cell and ask you to link its features to its job, so the method matters more than memorising one list.

bullets: **Differentiation** = the process by which a cell changes to become specialised for a particular function.
A **specialised cell** has a structure (shape, organelles, adaptations) that suits its function.
A cell that has not yet differentiated is **unspecialised**; **stem cells** are undifferentiated cells that can divide and then differentiate.
Differentiation happens as an organism **develops from a fertilised egg (zygote)**; the embryo divides by mitosis and the new cells then specialise.
Specialisation makes the organism more **efficient** because each cell type is adapted to do one job well, and different types of cells can **work together** in tissues and organs.
Differentiated cells usually **cannot change** into other cell types (in most animal cells), which is why mature animals mainly make more of the same type.
core.h: What is differentiation and why does it happen?
core.p: All cells in your body (apart from sex cells and red blood cells) contain the same full set of genetic instructions (the same DNA), yet a nerve cell looks and behaves nothing like a muscle cell. The reason is that during differentiation only some genes are switched on. The proteins that are made then give the cell its particular shape, organelles and function. Specialisation allows a multicellular organism to do many jobs at once efficiently: no single cell has to do everything.

bullets: In most **animals**, cells differentiate at an **early stage** and then lose the ability to become other cell types.
In **mature animals**, cell division is mostly restricted to **repair and replacement** (for example skin cells, blood cells), and the new cells are the same type.
In **plants**, **many types of cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life**.
Plant **meristem** tissue (at shoot and root tips) contains stem cells that differentiate into the plant cells needed for growth.
This explains why plants can be **cloned from cuttings** and why a plant can grow new roots from a stem.
In plants, differentiation produces cells such as xylem, phloem, root hair and palisade cells that are specialised for transport and exchange.
core.h: Animals versus plants: when does differentiation happen?
core.p: A key spec idea is that animal and plant cells differ in how long they keep the ability to differentiate. Most animal cells lose this ability early; in plants, many cells keep it throughout life, which is why a plant can regrow from a cutting.

bullets: Step 1: What is the **function** of the cell (e.g. carry a signal, absorb water, transport sugar)?
Step 2: Identify the **structural features** that are shown or described (shape, size, organelles, lack of organelles).
Step 3: Link each feature to function with the word **'so'** or **'which allows'**: 'many mitochondria so more energy from respiration'.
Step 4: Use specialist words: **surface area**, **diffusion**, **energy released by respiration**, **contract**, **transport**.

Common features and what they mean: lots of **mitochondria** = high energy demand; **large surface area** = fast absorption or exchange; **thin walls** = short diffusion distance; **long and thin** = reaches far or fits many in a space.
Prefer wording such as the feature **allows** or **enables** a process.
core.h: Linking structure to function: a method for any cell
core.p: In exams you may be shown a cell you have never seen. Use a consistent method: identify the cell's job, then look for features that help it do that job, and explain each feature in terms of what it does. A 'feature + function' pair earns a mark each.

bullets: **Many mitochondria in the middle section**: release energy from respiration for the tail to move the sperm.
**Acrosome** at the head: contains **digestive enzymes** to break down the outer layers of the egg cell so the sperm nucleus can enter.
**Haploid nucleus** (half the number of chromosomes): carries the father's genetic information; fuses with the egg nucleus to restore the full number.
**Streamlined head** reduces resistance, and the small size reduces the energy needed.
Sperm are made in very large numbers because few reach the egg.
Link: fertilisation and meiosis (gametes) in Biology topic 6.
core.p: The function of a sperm cell is to **carry the male's genetic information (a haploid nucleus) to the egg and fertilise it**. Every feature relates to getting to the egg and entering it. **Tail (flagellum)**: moves the sperm to swim towards the egg.

bullets: **Long axon**: carries the impulse over long distances (up to a metre).
**Dendrites** at the cell body and **dendrons**: branched ends that connect to other nerve cells, forming a network, and receive signals from many cells.
**Myelin sheath** (insulating fatty layer around the axon): speeds up the transmission of the nerve impulse.
**Synapses** at the ends (junctions with the next neurone): pass the signal by chemicals (neurotransmitters) diffusing across a gap.
Many **mitochondria** at the synapses release the energy needed to make the transmitter chemicals.
Link: nervous system, reflexes and reaction time practical (Biology topic 5 Homeostasis and response).
core.p: Nerve cells **carry electrical impulses** around the body, allowing rapid communication. They are long and branched so a single cell can carry signals over a large distance and connect to many other cells.

bullets: **Many mitochondria**: release energy from respiration to power contraction.
Store **glycogen**, which can be broken down to glucose for respiration to release energy.
Cells are **long** so they can contract a long way and are arranged in bundles for greater force.
Muscle cells contract and **relax in antagonistic pairs** (e.g. biceps and triceps), which is outside the spec but gives context.
Link: respiration and anaerobic respiration/oxygen debt in muscles (Biology topic 4.4).
core.p: The function of muscle cells is to **contract** (shorten) to bring about movement. Muscle cells are specialised to contract and then relax repeatedly. Contain special **protein fibres** that can **slide over each other**, causing the cell to **contract and shorten**; the cell lengthens when it relaxes.

bullets: **Thin cell wall**: short diffusion/osmosis distance so water enters quickly.
**Large permanent vacuole** containing cell sap with a **low water potential / high concentration of solutes**: helps water move in by osmosis.
**Many mitochondria**: release energy from respiration for **active transport** of mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) against a concentration gradient.
**No chloroplasts**: they are underground and receive no light, so don't photosynthesise.
Link: osmosis, active transport and transport in plants (Biology 4.1.3 and 4.3).
core.p: Root hair cells are found at the surface of plant roots and **absorb water (by osmosis) and mineral ions (by active transport) from the soil**. **Long, thin projection (the root hair)**: gives a **large surface area** for absorbing water and minerals.

bullets: Walls are strengthened with a substance called **lignin**, laid down in spirals or rings, which **supports the plant** and withstands the pressure of water.
Lignin makes the walls **waterproof**, so water moves along the tube without leaking out.
**Pits** in the walls allow water to move sideways between vessels.
Xylem moves water in **one direction only (upwards)** by the **transpiration stream**.
Link: transpiration, stomata and the effect of environmental factors on water uptake.
core.p: Xylem tissue **transports water and mineral ions** from the roots to the stem and leaves. The mature cells are dead and form long hollow tubes. Cells are joined end to end and the **end walls are broken down**, forming a continuous hollow tube with **no cytoplasm or nucleus** when mature, so water flows without obstruction.

bullets: Sieve tubes have **few organelles** and a very reduced cytoplasm, so there is little resistance to flow.
Each sieve tube element has a **companion cell** next to it, which has many **mitochondria** to release energy from respiration for active loading of sugars into the phloem.
Phloem transports substances **in both directions**, from where they are made to where they are used or stored.
Phloem is **living tissue**; xylem is **dead** when mature.
Link: photosynthesis (sugars made in leaves) and plant transport systems.
core.p: Phloem tissue **transports dissolved sugars (sucrose) and other substances** from the leaves to the rest of the plant. This is called **translocation**. Unlike xylem, phloem cells are living. Made of **sieve tube elements** joined end to end, with **sieve plates** (end walls with small pores) that allow sugary sap to pass through.

bullets: **Palisade mesophyll cells** (leaf): packed with **chloroplasts** containing chlorophyll for photosynthesis; **tall, thin shape** arranged near the top of the leaf for maximum light absorption.
**Red blood cells**: **biconcave disc** shape gives a large surface area for oxygen absorption; contain **haemoglobin** that binds oxygen; **no nucleus** leaves more space for haemoglobin.
**Guard cells**: change shape to open and close stomata (kidney-shaped).
**White blood cells**: can change shape to engulf pathogens (phagocytosis) and produce antibodies.
**Egg cell**: nutrients in cytoplasm to feed the embryo; the membrane changes after fertilisation to stop more sperm entering.
The pattern is always **structure (feature) → process → function**.
core.h: Other specialised cells you may meet
core.p: Exam questions often use cells from elsewhere in the spec. You will not be asked to recall them out of context, but you must be able to use the same feature-function method. Here are common examples. **Ciliated epithelial cells** (airways): **cilia** (tiny hairs) move mucus containing trapped dust and bacteria up and away from the lungs; **goblet cells** nearby make the mucus.

bullets: A **tissue** is a group of cells with a similar structure and function working together (e.g. muscular tissue).
An **organ** is a group of different tissues working together to perform a certain function (e.g. the stomach).
An **organ system** is a group of organs working together (e.g. the digestive system).
In plants, **xylem and phloem** form the vascular bundles; **palisade mesophyll** is the photosynthetic tissue in a leaf.
Specialised cells need to be **supplied with oxygen and nutrients** by transport systems because they are not in direct contact with the environment.
Specialisation improves efficiency but means cells depend on each other: damage to a tissue can affect the whole organism.
core.h: Specialised cells in tissues, organs and organ systems
core.p: Specialised cells do not work in isolation. They form **tissues**, which form **organs**, which form **organ systems**, which together make an organism. This shows why specialisation is important and links to the 'levels of organisation' topic.

bullets: **Embryonic stem cells** can become any type of cell; **adult stem cells** (such as bone marrow) form only certain cell types (e.g. blood cells).
**Meristem** tissue in plants is the source of stem cells throughout life.
Medical uses (replacing damaged cells) and issues are in section 4.1.2.3 (stem cells, covered in its own spec point).
Differentiation is why **mitosis** produces genetically identical cells which then become different through gene expression.
Higher tier thought: all body cells have the same genes, so differentiation is about **which genes are switched on**, not which genes are present.
In exams, 'cells in the embryo have differentiated' means they have become specialised and will no longer divide in the same way.
core.h: Differentiation, stem cells and links forward
core.p: Differentiation links to stem cells because **stem cells** are cells that have not yet differentiated and can become many different cell types. Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into any cell type; adult stem cells (e.g. in bone marrow) can differentiate into a limited range of cells.

exam: **State what differentiation is (1 mark)**: 'the process by which a cell changes to become specialised for its job'.
**Describe how a cell is adapted (2-3 marks)**: give a feature AND its function each time (e.g. 'many mitochondria to release energy for movement of the tail').
**Explain questions** need a link word: 'because', 'so that', 'which allows'. Features alone score nothing.
**Unfamiliar cell**: identify the function from the information, then link each feature given in the stem to it. Use the data given, not memory only.
**Compare xylem and phloem (3-4 marks)**: contents, living/dead, direction of flow, structure (lignin vs sieve plates).
**Animal vs plant (2 marks)**: most animal cells differentiate early, but many plant cells keep the ability throughout life.
**Correct terminology**: 'respiration releases energy' not 'makes energy'; 'osmosis' for water, 'active transport' for ions.
**Diagram labelling (1 mark each)**: look for the acrosome, nucleus, mitochondria and tail; read the labels carefully.
**6 mark extended answers**: choose 3 or more cells, give two adaptations each with explanation, and finish with how specialisation benefits the organism.
**Calculation links**: surface area to volume questions often use a root hair or cell as the example.

mistakes.r: Differentiation is the process by which a cell becomes specialised; division is mitosis.
The tail moves (propels) the sperm; the mitochondria supply the energy.
mistakes.w: Sperm have a tail so they can swim fast.

mistakes.r: Water enters by osmosis; mineral ions enter by active transport.
mistakes.w: Root hair cells absorb water by active transport.

mistakes.r: Xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem carries dissolved sugars.
mistakes.w: Xylem carries sugars; phloem carries water.

mistakes.r: Mature xylem cells are dead, hollow and have lignin-strengthened walls.
mistakes.w: Xylem cells are living with a nucleus.

mistakes.r: Mitochondria are the site of respiration, which releases energy.
Say why: a large surface area allows faster absorption or exchange of substances.
mistakes.w: A large surface area is useful.

mistakes.r: Most animal cells differentiate early; in mature animals, division is mainly for repair and replacement. Many plant cells can differentiate throughout life.
mistakes.w: Animal cells can differentiate all through life.

mistakes.r: All cells have the same genes; differentiation depends on which genes are switched on.

summary: AQA expects you to explain that differentiation is the process by which a cell becomes specialised for a particular function, to know that most animal cells differentiate early whereas many plant cells keep this ability throughout life, and to explain how the structure of specialised cells (sperm, nerve, muscle, root hair, xylem, phloem and others) is related to their function. It matters because it underpins levels of organisation, stem cells and transport, and unfamiliar-cell questions test the feature-to-function method.

terms.d: The process by which a cell changes to become specialised for a particular function.
A cell with a structure adapted to carry out a particular function.
A cell that has not yet differentiated and has no particular function.
An undifferentiated cell that can divide and differentiate into other cell types.
Plant tissue at shoot and root tips containing stem cells that can differentiate throughout life.
A group of cells with a similar structure and function.
A group of different tissues that work together to perform a certain function.
A group of organs working together to perform a certain function.
Part of the sperm head containing digestive enzymes to break down the egg's outer layer.
A nucleus with half the normal number of chromosomes, as in gametes.
The long part of a nerve cell that carries electrical impulses.
Fatty insulating layer around some axons that speeds up impulse transmission.
The junction between two neurones where a signal passes by chemicals.
A strong, waterproof substance in xylem walls that provides support.
The perforated end wall between phloem sieve tube elements.
A cell next to a phloem sieve tube element with many mitochondria providing energy.
The movement of dissolved sugars in the phloem from sources to where they are needed.
A specialised root cell with a long projection to absorb water and minerals.

worked.ans: Mitochondria release energy from respiration. In a sperm cell the energy is needed for the tail to move so that the sperm can swim to the egg. In a muscle cell the energy is needed for the protein fibres to contract so that the muscle can shorten and cause movement.
worked.q: A sperm cell and a muscle cell both contain many mitochondria. Explain why each cell needs many mitochondria. (4 marks)
steps: Identify what mitochondria do: site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy.
Sperm: energy for the tail to move so the sperm swims to the egg.
Muscle: energy for protein fibres to slide and contract the muscle.

worked.ans: Xylem transports water and mineral ions. Mature xylem cells are dead with no cytoplasm or nucleus and the end walls are broken down to form a hollow tube so that water flows without obstruction. The walls contain lignin, which strengthens and waterproofs them to support the plant. Phloem transports dissolved sugars. Sieve tube elements have sieve plates with pores so that sugars can pass through. They have few organelles and reduced cytoplasm so there is less resistance to flow. Companion cells have many mitochondria that release energy for loading sugars into the phloem. Xylem moves water upwards only, while phloem can move sugars in both directions.
worked.q: Describe how xylem and phloem cells are adapted for their functions. (6 marks)
steps: Xylem: dead, hollow, lignin, no end walls.
Phloem: sieve plates, companion cells, living.
Finish with direction of movement and what is transported.

worked.ans: The long thin root hair gives a large surface area, so more water can be absorbed by osmosis. The cell contains many mitochondria which release energy from respiration, so mineral ions can be absorbed by active transport against a concentration gradient.
worked.q: Root hair cells are specialised for absorbing water and minerals. Explain two adaptations. (4 marks)
steps: Pick two features and link each to function.
Mention the transport process (osmosis, active transport).
